props.title: You and Me
lines: You and I can look at the same price and be playing different games.
Bubbles form when short-term traders set prices that long-term owners then treat as wisdom.

rows.v: Cisco stock rose 300% in 1999 to $60 a share. Market value about $600 billion.
At $60, a momentum trader can be right for a week. A 30-year owner needed a different math.
The average mutual fund had about 120% annual turnover — many 'investors' were not investing.
Identify your game. Do not take cues from people playing a different one.

props.title: Do not import another player's scoreboard

rows.v: Cisco rose 300% in 1999 to $60. Valuation about $600 billion.
A one-week momentum trader can be right at $60. That does not make $60 a 30-year entry.
Average mutual fund turnover about 120% a year — many holders were not 'investors.'
Short-term players set the print. Long-term owners treat the print as wisdom. That is how bubbles recruit.

props.title: Name your time horizon out loud
items: Write whether you are playing weeks, years, or decades before you copy a price take.
Hot takes from a different game are not information. They are someone else's payoff function.

rows.v: Short-term traders can be right about a print that is nonsense for a thirty-year holder.
Cisco at sixty dollars after a three hundred percent year was a trader's win and an owner's trap.
About one hundred twenty percent average fund turnover meant many 'holders' were not investing.
Bubbles recruit long-term money with short-term scoreboards. Name your clock before you copy.
If you cannot say whether you are playing weeks or decades, you are playing someone else's game.
